messages.subject: Snap shot point transects
parts:
Dear users,



I am currently collecting density estimates of small passerine birds but ha=
ve also been looking into alternatives to point counts (over 2x2 min period=
s). I have read about the snap-shot method and was wondering if anyone has =
used this and, if so, could they provide a description of the methodology? =
I have read through a few papers concerning this method but cannot find a p=
articularly in-depth description of its use. Any advice would be greatly ap=
preciated.



Kind regards,



John Norrey

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Snap shot point transects
parts:
John, I'll send separately pdf's of the following papers:

Buckland, S.T. 2006. Point transect surveys for songbirds: robust
methodologies. /The Auk/ *123*, 345-357.

Buckland, S.T., Marsden, S.J. and Green, R.E. 2008. Estimating bird
abundance: making methods work. /Bird Conservation International/ *18*,
S91-S108.


You will probably consider these to not be 'particularly in-depth'
though - that is essentially because there is not a lot to say about
it. Conceptually, distance sampling is a snapshot method. For species
where individuals move around very little, you can afford to stretch
this snapshot moment out over a longer time period. For very mobile
species, you cannot. The problem is that you want to ensure that
probability of detection at the point is certain (unless you use
mark-recapture methods), while at the same time recording positions of
birds as if they're frozen at their initial location. Give them time to
move around, and you'll record new birds coming on to the plot as well
as ones initially there that have since moved on, and overestimate
density on the plot. It's easy to say you should record locations at a
snapshot moment only, but difficult to achieve, while ensuring that det
prob at the point is one. In e.g. open, temperate woodland, for
breeding surveys of many songbird species at least, this is achievable.
Dense rainforest is another proposition.

Steve Buckland
